game-port-deduce.intro: From the scan output, name the service or the behaviour.

challenges.q: Port 22 open on a Linux host. Service?
Ports 139 and 445 open on a Windows host. Service?
nmap reports 22/tcp filtered and 80/tcp open. What does filtered mean?
Port 3389 open. Service?
A SYN scan of UDP port 161 returns a response, port 53 also responds. What two services?
nmap -O reports the target has a TTL of 64 in replies. Likely OS family?
challenges.hint: 64 is the default TTL for one family

challenges.q: Port 8080 open serving an HTTP banner but the main site is on 80. What is 8080 likely?
challenges.hint: Alternate HTTP port, often management or app server

challenges.q: All 1000 scanned ports report closed with identical reset behaviour, but the host pings. What does this suggest?
a: No services on those ports, the host is up
challenges.why: Closed with consistent resets and a live host means the scan worked and nothing is listening.

game-beacon-hunt.intro: Find the periodic callout in the quiet traffic.

challenges.q: Hosts A, B, C, D all contact many destinations. Host C contacts one destination every 60 seconds with a constant 512-byte request. Which is beaconing?
challenges.why: Regular interval plus constant size to a single destination is beaconing.

challenges.q: Why is beaconing detectable even over TLS?
a: Timing and packet size patterns survive encryption
challenges.why: Metadata is unencrypted, and regularity is the tell.

challenges.q: Traffic is to the same CDN the company legitimately uses, at regular intervals. Can this be C2?
a: Yes, abusing allowed services is a common evasion technique
challenges.why: Blending into permitted destinations defeats naive allowlisting.

challenges.q: Which interval pattern is most suspicious?
a: Exactly 300 seconds every time, day and night
challenges.why: Machine-precise regularity around the clock implies automation, not a human.

challenges.q: A host makes DNS queries where the subdomain is a base64-encoded blob that changes each time, to the same domain. Assessment?
challenges.why: High-entropy changing subdomains encode data in query names.

challenges.q: Why does jitter reduce detection chance?
a: It breaks the exact regularity detectors rely on
challenges.why: Jitter makes interval analysis harder, though volume still betrays it.

game-exploit-chain.intro: Sequence the steps from port scan to shell.

challenges.q: Order a basic exploitation chain.
items: Upgrade the shell to a TTY
challenges.why: Reconnaissance, identification, research, exploit, catch, then make it usable.

challenges.q: Order the post-exploitation steps immediately after landing on Linux.
items: Enumerate the host and current privileges
challenges.why: Stabilise first so everything else works, then enumerate before acting.

challenges.q: Order these by whether they run before or after gaining a foothold: least privilege needed first.
items: Requesting a service ticket for a SPN as a domain user
challenges.why: Passive reconnaissance needs nothing; a ticket needs any account; a kernel exploit needs local access; DCSync needs replication rights.

challenges.q: Order a web attack chain from discovery to impact.
challenges.why: Confirm by hand before automating, then escalate impact from data to access.

challenges.q: Order the defence-evasion considerations by how much they reduce detection.
items: Blend timing to match normal traffic
Adopt attacker behaviour indistinguishable from legitimate admin activity
challenges.why: Hash changes are trivial to detect through; behavioural mimicry is the hardest detection problem there is.

challenges.q: Order these Web vulnerabilities by typical time to weaponise, fastest first.
items: Default credentials on an exposed admin panel
SQL injection on a login form
Chained privilege escalation via misconfigured AD
challenges.why: Default credentials take minutes; AD chains take days of patient enumeration.

game-ids-triage.intro: Real attack or false positive? Decide and justify.

challenges.q: Alert: GET /?id=1 UNION SELECT 1,2,3 from an external IP. Assessment?
a: Likely real injection attempt, high priority
challenges.why: A UNION SELECT payload in a parameter is a deliberate injection attempt.

challenges.q: Alert: outbound SMB from a workstation to an internal file server during business hours. Assessment?
challenges.why: Normal protocol, normal destination, normal time. The same event at 03:00 to an external host would be different.

challenges.q: Alert: a service account logs in at 03:12 from a country you do not operate in. Assessment?
challenges.why: A service account does not travel. This is a strong compromise indicator.

challenges.q: Alert: port scan from an internal vulnerability scanner IP that runs weekly. Assessment?
a: Expected activity from a known scanner, low priority, but confirm schedules match
challenges.why: Known scanning infrastructure is expected, though you verify the schedule.

challenges.q: Alert: lsass process memory access by a non-security tool. Assessment?
challenges.why: Reading lsass outside EDR or antivirus is credential theft.

challenges.q: Alert: many 404s to a nonsense path from one IP over ten minutes. Assessment?
challenges.why: Likely directory brute forcing, which is an attempt rather than a breach.

challenges.q: Alert: a scheduled nightly PowerShell task that uploads a report to a vendor. Assessment?
a: Likely legitimate but worth verifying against approved change records
challenges.why: Legitimate scheduled automation looks identical to malicious automation, so you verify.

challenges.q: Alert: DNS TXT queries for long random subdomains, hundreds per minute, one host. Assessment?
challenges.why: High-volume high-entropy DNS to one domain is exfiltration.
